title: Prevalence and factors associated with puerperal sepsis at LUTH
content:
by Salma M. Baines, Kimberley R. Kurehwatira, Chileleko Siakabanze, Emmanuel Yumba, Prince Mulambo, David N. Masta, Nestorine N. Ngongo, Natasha Chishala, Emmanuel O. Riwo, Emmanuel L. Luwaya, Katongo H. Mutengo, David Chisompola, Hanzooma Hatwiko, Martin Chakulya, Lukundo Siame, Bislom C. Mweene, Sepiso K. Masenga

Puerperal sepsis remains a leading cause of maternal mortality in low-resource settings, contributing to 19% of Zambia’s estimated 252 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. Despite its significant burden, localized data on risk factors remain sparse. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and determinants of puerperal sepsis at Livingstone University Teaching Hospital (LUTH), a tertiary referral centre in Southern Zambia. A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using medical records of 460 postpartum women admitted to LUTH between January 2023 and December 2024. Data on demographic, clinical, and laboratory variables were extracted using a standardized form in REDCap. Puerperal sepsis was defined as a genital tract infection occurring within six weeks postpartum (WHO criteria). Descriptive statistics and multivariable logistic regression models were employed to analyse associations. The prevalence of puerperal sepsis was 5.4% (25/460). In adjusted analyses, elevated white blood cell count (AOR: 1.30 per unit increase; 95% CI: 1.13–1.50; p < 0.001) and lower haemoglobin levels (AOR 0.71, 95% CI: 0.54–0.95; p = 0.019) were independent predictors of puerperal sepsis. Postpartum haemorrhage, antenatal visit frequency, maternal hypotension and multiple births were not significantly associated with puerperal sepsis after adjustment. Compared to non-sepsis cases, sepsis cases were more likely to involve younger maternal age (median: 22 vs. 26 years; p = 0.048) and prolonged labour (median: 11 vs. 9 hours; p = 0.044). Elevated white blood cell count, and lower haemoglobin levels were significantly associated with puerperal sepsis. These findings highlight the potential value of routine haematological assessment in identifying mothers who may require closer clinical monitoring. Strengthening routine monitoring and timely intervention may help reduce the burden of puerperal sepsis and improve maternal outcomes. However, given the limited number of outcome events, the findings should be interpreted with caution, and further studies with larger sample sizes are recommended.
